readingInstruction: Read Titus 1:1-3:15. This short letter to Titus in Crete shows how sound doctrine and good works belong together. Notice the repeated phrases “sound doctrine” and “good works,” and the gospel summaries in 2:11-14 and 3:4-7.
settingTheScene: Titus was one of Paul’s trusted coworkers, a Gentile convert. Paul left him on the island of Crete to put the churches in order and appoint elders in every town. The Cretans had a reputation for dishonesty and laziness (even one of their own poets said so), and false teachers were upsetting households. Paul writes to give Titus authority and instructions, and in doing so gives some of the clearest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament.
observation: “They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works” (1:16).
“But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine” (2:1).
“For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people” (2:11).
“Waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:13).
“Who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (2:14).
“He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (3:5).
“The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works” (3:8).
“But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless” (3:9).
interpretation:
Paul opens with a long greeting that sets the gospel in eternity: he is a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ for the sake of the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth, “in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began.” Then the task: appoint elders (covered on Day 811) and silence the empty talkers who upset whole families. The Cretans, as one of their own prophets said, were “always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” Titus is to rebuke them sharply that they may be sound in the faith. “To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; their very minds and consciences are defiled. They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works.”

Chapter 2 gives instruction for each group in the church: older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and slaves. The goal in all cases is to “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” and keep the word of God from being reviled. Doctrine and life belong together. Then the gospel as the basis for this life: “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works.” Grace does not excuse sin but trains us out of it. Christ is called “our great God and Savior,” one of the plain statements of his deity. He gave himself to redeem and to purify.

In chapter 3, Paul tells Titus to remind believers to be submissive to rulers, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people. Why? Because “we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures.” Then the second great summary: “But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.” Here the Father, Son, and Spirit all work for our salvation. It is entirely mercy; it is new birth; it makes us heirs.

Paul concludes: insist on these things, so that believers will devote themselves to good works. Avoid foolish controversies. Warn a divisive person once, then twice, and then have nothing to do with him. The letter ends with practical greetings and the blessing, “Grace be with you all.”
connection: Ephesians 2:8-10 also joins salvation by grace with good works. Romans 6:1-4 answers whether grace excuses sin. John 3:3-8 and 1 Peter 1:3 speak of new birth. Romans 5:1-2 and 8:17 speak of justification and heirs. Deuteronomy 7:6 and 1 Peter 2:9 speak of a people for God’s own possession. 2 Peter 1:1 and John 20:28 also call Christ God. Matthew 28:19 names Father, Son, and Spirit. Romans 13:1-7 speaks of rulers. James 2:14-26 joins faith and works. Matthew 5:16 speaks of good works glorifying the Father.
application:
Read 2:11-14 slowly. Underline each work of grace: it appears, saves, trains, redeems, purifies.

Pick one “good work” you can do for someone this week as a fruit of grace, and do it.

Remember the person you were before Christ (3:3) the next time you are tempted to be harsh with someone.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for redeeming you and purifying a people for himself.
Ask him to make you zealous for good works.
Ask him to keep you from foolish arguments.
